title: Checkpoint: Traps in Our Reasoning
objective: After this level you can name the reasoning traps that catch careful people and a habit that counters each one.
summary: Feynman's first principle, don't fool yourself, ties the chapter together. Each trap has a habit that counters it: hunt for the no, switch sides, draw the target first, ask compared with what.

cards.headline: Richard Feynman's first rule for thinking: don't fool yourself.
cards.body: The physicist gave that advice to new Caltech graduates in 1974, and added that you are the easiest person to fool. Nine levels of traps later, you know exactly why. Let's line them up.

cards.headline: Leaning over backwards
cards.body: Feynman described scientific integrity as a kind of utter honesty, a leaning over backwards. If you do an experiment, report everything that might make it invalid. If you put out a theory, put down the facts that disagree with it as well as those that agree. That's Bacon's negative instance, turned into a rule for honest work: the misses get counted along with the hits.

cards.headline: Every trap in this chapter has a habit that counters it

items.label: What you notice
points: Confirmation bias: go looking for a no
Texas sharpshooter: draw the target first

items.label: How you judge
points: Motivated reasoning: ask "Must I?" of both sides
Blind spot: judge yourself by your behavior

items.label: What counts as a reason
points: Nature or tradition: ask why, not where from

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: How confirmation bias and motivated reasoning bend evidence, and the habits that straighten it.
Why a double standard hides from the inside, and how the switch-sides test catches it.
What makes nature, tradition, perfection or confidence weak reasons on their own.
Why everyone has a bias blind spot, and why being smart doesn't remove it.

questions.prompt: In his 1974 Caltech address, what did Richard Feynman call the first principle?

options.label: Always trust the experts
options.rationale: His principle points inward, at yourself.

options.label: Never publish a failed experiment
options.rationale: He urged reporting what could make results invalid.

options.label: Science is mostly luck
options.rationale: He said nothing of the kind.

questions.explanation: Feynman: the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.

questions.prompt: Why did Feynman want scientists to report the facts that disagree with their theory?

options.label: So the misses get counted along with the hits
So their papers would be longer
options.rationale: Length isn't the point; honesty is.

options.label: So other scientists would stop checking
So the theory would always be rejected
options.rationale: Disagreeing facts are weighed, not automatic vetoes.

questions.explanation: Reporting what disagrees is Bacon's negative instance as a working rule: count the misses with the hits.

questions.prompt: Match each trap with the habit that counters it.
questions.explanation: Counter confirmation bias by going looking for a no, and the Texas sharpshooter by drawing the target first. Counter a double standard by switching sides, and the blind spot by judging yourself by your behavior.

questions.prompt: The question _____ deflates the perfect-solution fallacy.

options.label: "Who benefits from this?"
options.rationale: A fair question, but not the one for this trap.

questions.explanation: Demsetz: compare real alternatives, not reality with a perfect ideal.

questions.prompt: In the 1984 study by Lord, Lepper and Preston, what reduced bias more than urging people to be fair?

options.label: Reading about the topic for longer
options.rationale: The study compared considering the opposite with fairness instructions.

options.label: Getting them to consider the opposite
Letting them discuss it in groups
options.rationale: Group talk wasn't the tested strategy.

questions.explanation: Considering the opposite had a greater corrective effect than instructions to be fair and unbiased.
